newsitem.title: USA: AT&T stock undervalued -- AT&T CEO Allen.
newsitem.headline: AT&T stock undervalued -- AT&T CEO Allen.

text.p: The Chairman of AT&T Corp said Tuesday his company's stock price is undervalued and that his top priority is to boost the share's value.

"I think it's a cheap stock," Robert Allen said during a question and answer session after a speech to the National Press Club. Without giving details, Allen added that he recently bought some of the company's stock and that he had no plans to sell shares.
"I'm in the buy mode, not the sell mode," he said.
Allen said that a top priority this year is to clarify to the financial community AT&T strategy so that the stock price can move up to the level "where it ought to be."
Allen said that the company's top three priorities for 1997 were value creation. "Value creation is number one, number two and number three," he said.
Allen said that the new AT&T, following its three-way breakup last year, is undervalued in the marketplace.
Speaking on other subjects, Allen said that AT&T has completed more than 52 "interconnection" cases in 34 states covering more than 80 percent of the local access lines in the nation.
Interconnection refers to an agreement to hook up to a local phone company's network to provide local service, as called for by the Telecommunications Act of 1996.

Most of the agreements fall within the guidelines laid out by the Federal Communications Commission, although a U.S. appeals court last year suspended the FCC rules and turned over much of the decision-making authority to state regulators.

Allen pledged that when AT&T is permitted to offer both local and long-distance phone service throughout the country on the terms it has been seeking, "we will offer those services at prices no greater and probably less than what customers are paying separately for those services right now."

But Allen declined to pledge that the company would pass on to consumers any reductions it sees in the rates it pays foreign phone monopolies to terminate overseas calls. The FCC has made it a top priority to reduce the accounting rates charged by state-run foreign carriers and currently has a proposal out for public comment.

Allen pledged to pass along any reductions that occur in the access charges that long-distance carriers pay local phone companies in this country to hook up to their local network. The FCC is now considering how to reduce access charges.

"In fact, if we get a clear indication that access charge reductions are going to happen, we'll pass the reductions through to our customers even before we see them, as we've done in the past," Allen said.
